title: Minotaur - arcade dungeon crawling action!
body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9dFDeUNHViY

Daniel (@dungeondive) takes a chance on Minotaur, a small-box cooperative crawl by Jared Garcia from a company he had never heard of, and comes away glad he did. He opens by wondering why the Theseus myth, arguably the foundation story of the whole genre, turns up so rarely in dungeon games.

One to four players (solo means running two heroes) pick from eight classes with distinct kits: a warlock who drains kills into healing, a ranger with spread fire and a shared target token, a warrior who bashes walls, a rogue who backstabs and cloaks, and so on. Everyone can disarm traps, dispel magical barriers, and break physical ones, but not equally well, so pairing a wizard with a rogue leaves you unable to knock down a brick wall. Daniel's favourite pairing is warrior and wizard.

The labyrinth is a three-by-three grid of cards that scrolls like an old console screen. Step off one edge and the opposite row falls away, taking every monster on it, and every item too, including any medallion halves you left behind. Collecting both halves of three medallions is how you finally banish the Minotaur, who otherwise respawns like Nemesis in Resident Evil 3 and grows stronger the closer you get. Each hero carries one item, so much of the game is pack-mule logistics. Daniel calls it Gauntlet on cardboard: no story, no loot to speak of, but sharp choices, a quick setup, and a small price.

----

Minotaur's scrolling labyrinth throws away everything on the row you leave behind, monsters and medallion halves alike. Is that kind of hard trade-off what a small-box crawl needs to feel like more than a filler?
